mappings.note: Explain the sense of the line about youths far from life's struggle finding the world charming -- the young-versus-old outlook, C-3.1-LO-4, not the proverb outcome C-4.3-LO-3.
Explain the line that no age ever lacked the need for reform -- the continuity-of-social-reform half of C-3.1-LO-4.
Today's young will grow old and dream of past glory -- the generational-outlook analysis, C-3.1-LO-4.
Explain the claim that a short essay beats a long one -- a statement about the nibandh form, so C-1.1-LO-4 (essay definition and genre), not C-1.2's style analysis.
Which topics you found easy or hard to write on, and why -- the student's own reasoned view, C-2.1. Not C-1.1-LO-5, which is the author's state of mind, not the reader's.
Research what Buddha, Mahavira, Nagarjuna, Shankaracharya, Kabir and Nanak did for society -- evidence for the continuity of social reform, C-3.1-LO-4.
Find and write about people and bodies working on women's education, environment and disability today -- a reasoned engagement with social issues, C-2.1.
Hold a class debate on the generation gap: C-3.1-LO-4 for the young-versus-old analysis it is about, C-2.1 for the reasoned oral expression the debate format demands.

The word 'nibandh' across Eighth Schedule languages plus the sentence in your mother tongue -- Indian linguistic diversity, so C-4.3 at competency level and CG-4. Neither C-4.3-LO-3 (lokokti) nor LO-4 (samas, upsarg-pratyay) applies.
Read Agyeya's 'Main kyon likhta hoon' alongside this text -- both are about the writer's inner state when the question of what to write arises, C-1.1-LO-5.

Look up Banabhatta, Sriharsha, Khusro, Gandhi, Gardiner, Shakespeare and Montaigne. The list is the essay-method comparison the text runs on, so C-3.1-LO-3; C-4.2 does not fit because half the names are not from Indian literature.
Who wrote 'Kya Likhoon'. Authorship recall, which no LO of this chapter states, so C-1.1 at competency level.
Bakshi's birthplace. Biographical recall, no LO covers it, so C-1.1 at competency level.
Gardiner says writing needs a particular state of mind -- exactly the mental condition of C-1.1-LO-5.
What arises in the mind in that writing state (an aaveg) -- C-1.1-LO-5.
Fill in 'any khoonti will do to hang a hat on'. The peg image is the text's vehicle for subject-versus-feeling, so C-1.1-LO-6.
What the hat-and-peg example teaches: bhav is the real thing, vishay is not -- C-1.1-LO-6, the subject/feeling distinction.
The author's real difficulty is never having felt that state of mind -- C-1.1-LO-5.
What Namita told him to write on -- the commission that sets off the 'what shall I write' predicament, C-1.1-LO-5.
What Amita asked him to write on -- the same commissioning situation, C-1.1-LO-5.
How many pages each essay had to run to -- a detail of the writing predicament, C-1.1-LO-5.
Assertion-reason: he first consulted the acharyas of nibandh-shastra to learn what an ideal essay is -- the genre-definition outcome C-1.1-LO-4.
Why a short essay is held better -- a principle of the essay form, C-1.1-LO-4.
The two chief limbs of an essay (samagri and shaili) -- essay-genre knowledge, C-1.1-LO-4.
He had two hours for both essays -- part of the pressured situation behind 'what shall I write', C-1.1-LO-5.
Gardiner leaves the titling to his friend. Titling is the subject-side of the subject/feeling split the essay argues, so C-1.1-LO-6.
Statements on Gardiner's and Shakespeare's trouble with titles, and 'As You Like It' -- the same subject-versus-content theme, C-1.1-LO-6.
Why distant drums sound sweet -- the harshness does not carry. This is the lokokti outcome C-4.3-LO-3 stated by name.
What happens to those sitting beside the drum -- the folk experience behind the proverb, C-4.3-LO-3.
What the distant listener imagines on hearing the drum -- still the proverb's folk experience, C-4.3-LO-3.

The three things said to be mingled in the drumbeat (anand ka kalrav, utsav ka pramod, prem ka sangeet). This item turns on the author's imagery, so the bimb competency C-1.2, not the proverb outcome.
Distance hides the harshness of reality -- the proverb's general lesson, C-4.3-LO-3.
How the world looks to youths far from its struggle -- the young-versus-old outlook, C-3.1-LO-4.
Statements on the young pulling the future forward and the old the past -- the generational-difference analysis, C-3.1-LO-4.
The young back revolution, the old guard past glory -- C-3.1-LO-4.
Why the present is always kshubdh, given both generations -- C-3.1-LO-4.
Which reformer's name is NOT in the text's list -- recall serving the continuity-of-reform thread, C-3.1-LO-4.
When reform ended in human history: never -- the continuity of social reform, C-3.1-LO-4.
Assertion-reason: yesterday's reforms are today's faults, hence life is progressive -- C-3.1-LO-4.
What the makers of progressive literature believe about future glory -- the generational argument, C-3.1-LO-4.
The sense of 'progressive literature too will become a monument of the past' -- C-3.1-LO-4.
Both generations' dreams are sweet because distant drums sound sweet -- the closing return to the lokokti, C-4.3-LO-3.
What writing one essay costs him -- thought, worry and labour; the author's writing condition, C-1.1-LO-5.
What Gardiner wrote of Shakespeare: naming the plays was harder than writing them -- the title-versus-substance point, C-1.1-LO-6.
Statements about Montaigne's essays -- the Montaigne-method outcome C-3.1-LO-3.
How the old find memories of their youth -- the older generation's outlook, C-3.1-LO-4.
Fill in: the drum's harshness becomes 'atyant madhur' for those far off -- the proverb's own wording, C-4.3-LO-3.
The wide sense given to 'distant drums sound sweet' -- people prize what is far off or past. The lokokti outcome C-4.3-LO-3.
What the essay says of Senapati making his verse obscure -- part of the East-versus-West method contrast that C-3.1-LO-3 covers.
Best conclusion about essay writing: there is no one fixed method -- a judgement about the nibandh form, C-1.1-LO-4.
Gardiner's special state of mind for writing -- C-1.1-LO-5.
The core point of the hat-and-peg example -- subject versus feeling, C-1.1-LO-6.
He agrees with Gardiner yet is stuck -- his own mental difficulty, C-1.1-LO-5.
Which topics Namita and Amita set him -- the commissioning situation, C-1.1-LO-5.
Why a scholar says an essay should be short -- essay-form principle, C-1.1-LO-4.
Gardiner's hardest task was the title -- the title/substance distinction, C-1.1-LO-6.
In what connection 'As You Like It' is cited -- the difficulty of naming versus the writing itself, C-1.1-LO-6.
In what context Banabhatta and Sriharsha appear -- the older Indian composition method set against Montaigne's, C-3.1-LO-3.
The chief feature of Montaigne's essay method -- C-3.1-LO-3 names Montaigne directly.
The Amir Khusro anecdote of four women's wishes. It is the model the author borrows to escape his own predicament, so C-1.1-LO-5 rather than the Montaigne-comparison LO.
Explain the sense of 'door ke dhol suhavne hote hain' as the essay does -- C-4.3-LO-3.
Why both the young and the old are shown discontented with the present -- C-3.1-LO-4.
How the closing ties the proverb to social reform: C-4.3-LO-3 for the lokokti, C-3.1-LO-4 for the reform argument it is joined to.

What the essay's aatmaparak style is and what it gives the piece. This asks the student to ANALYSE the style, so C-1.2; C-2.2-LO-4 is the nearest sibling but it asks the student to WRITE an aatmaparak essay, which this does not.
The two chief limbs of an essay and the author's difficulty with both -- essay-genre knowledge, C-1.1-LO-4.
The author's view on making an outline and why he could not: LO-4 for the essay-craft principle, LO-5 for his own state. Not C-2.2-LO-3, which has the STUDENT build an outline and write from it.
How adopting Khusro's method halved his difficulty -- his resolution of the 'what shall I write' problem, C-1.1-LO-5.
In which contexts the proverb is explained and its universal force -- C-4.3-LO-3.
The view taken of social reform and the line 'neither faults nor reforms end' -- C-3.1-LO-4.
Compare the Eastern and Western essay methods as the text sets them out -- C-3.1-LO-3, the Montaigne-versus-this-author comparison.
How Bakshi searches for the ideal way to write an essay, plus the piece's literary features: LO-4 for the genre question, C-1.2 for the style analysis.
